item.title: γ₁₁: Contact Geometry — the macadamias 0001, 0014, 0059 and 0015
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2827
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: The root paper of this series reduces the value $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ of the Hermite constant to a statement about chains of lattices $L\supset M\supset N$ of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member lies, in the sense of Voronoi, over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms; the $\gamma_{11}$ paper excludes all of them but ten, the macadamias. This paper settles four macadamias, the forms 0001:010488327, 0014:001749549, 0059:016902802 and 0015:030291998, by one method: the geometry of the contacts of the form. A section frame of short dual vectors forces the first gluing of $M$ over $N$ to lie near one of finitely many coherent centres; at such a centre the rank-10 metric is compared with an explicit reference lattice, whose Delaunay cells and contact identities give a uniform bound on its covering radius; and a primitive-extension inequality turns that bound into $\det L\ge 972$. The proof is computer-assisted: every finite check it uses is stated as a Computational result with the records of the certificate archive that certify it, and all comparisons are between explicit rational numbers.

item.title: A Focus on Hermite Constant 11
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2826
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper assembles the dimension-eleven argument in a series on the Hermite constants in dimensions ten, eleven and twelve. The root paper reduces a hypothetical lattice of minimum 4 and determinant below 972 to a chain of sections of ranks eleven, ten and nine. Its rank-nine section is marked by a perfect form below an explicit determinant cutoff. The global finite computation leaves 4 487 813 candidate forms and excludes all but ten by certificates. We state the mathematical content of these certificates, describe their data and checking rules, and prove why every valid certificate excludes the corresponding form. The four formats are trace, domain, glue and tree certificates; each tree must cover its entire stated domain. One of the ten remaining cases, 0052:005247066, is treated here by a complete gluing cover. Five companion papers settle the other nine. We also prove the common inequalities used by those local arguments. The resulting bound is $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$, conditional on the attributed rank-nine classification, the rank-ten census and the stated global and local finite checks.

item.title: The Hermite Constants in Dimensions 10, 11 and 12
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2825
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper introduces a series of seven papers establishing $\gamma_{10}^{10}=4^{10}/768$, $\gamma_{11}^{11}=4^{11}/972$ and $\gamma_{12}=4/\sqrt{3}$, under the attributed classification of perfect forms of rank nine and the explicitly stated computational inputs. The argument treats the dimensions in order. In dimension ten, a section orthogonal to a shortest dual vector is compared with a perfect form. A completed exact census leaves three possible reference forms, and matrix inequalities exclude a determinant below 768 in each case. In dimension eleven, two successive sections give a chain of ranks eleven, ten and nine. The dimension-ten bound controls the determinant of the last section. The verified global census and preliminary certificates reduce the problem to ten local cases: nine are treated in five companion papers, and one in “A Focus on Hermite Constant 11”. The local arguments combine contact geometry, section bounds and finite rational covers. Mordell’s inequality then gives the dimension-twelve upper bound, matched by the Coxeter–Todd lattice. We prove the common reduction, explain the dependency between the papers, and state exactly which finite assertions must be checked. The accompanying Lean development verifies the complete analytic deduction from those inputs; external exact checkers verify the large certificate data.

item.title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2824
Authors: Shafi Goldwasser, Yael Tauman Kalai
Summary: Incrementally verifiable computation ($\IVC$) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. In the context of AI safety, the need for incremental verification is particularly important, as AI systems interact with users over time and perform further computation after each interaction. However, standard $\IVC$ schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise. Indeed, the UK AISI Alignment Team~\cite{IrvingM25} emphasizes that verification methods for AI safety should accommodate access to external information and human judgment. This is the topic of this paper.
We construct $\IVC$ schemes for {\em oracle-aided} computations under the Learning with Errors ($\LWE$) assumption by first constructing succinct non-interactive arguments ($\SNARG$s), and then extending them to the incremental setting. We consider the following two settings, where below, $\lambda$ is the security parameter, $n$ is the input length, and $T$, $S$, and $Q$ are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds. \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robust computations.} For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an $\varepsilon$-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct {\em privately verifiable} $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$. For $\IVC$, the corresponding robustness condition is imposed on the claimed configuration. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T,1/\varepsilon)$, and verification uses $O(\lambda/\varepsilon)$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$s with public parameters of length $o(n)$, and $o(Q)$ verifier oracle queries.
\item \textbf{Signed oracles.} For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$ without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T)$. For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$, we remove the dependence on $S$, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$.
\end{itemize} All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness. Sub-exponential hardness of $\LWE$ suffices for all constructions; polynomial hardness suffices in the deterministic signed-oracle setting when $T$ is polynomially bounded in $\lambda$. All cryptographic assumptions are required to hold even given access to the underlying oracle.

item.title: Revisiting the Security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2823
Authors: Tingting Guo, Peng Wang, Shuping Mao, Yan Jia, Jiadong Han
Summary: We revisit the security of OleF, t-OleF, and \olaef\ and identify two independent security flaws. First, we establish a mask-compensation relation between continuation and termination processing in OleF and t-OleF. Exploiting this relation, we construct a two-encryption-query distinguisher against OleF with advantage $1-2^{-2n}$. We further give two concrete AXU hash families for which the same attack applies to t-OleF, revealing flaws in the original DOSPRP and SPRTOP security proofs. We extend these attacks to \olaef\ through valid encodings, breaking its privacy and integrity. In particular, the integrity forgery succeeds with probability $1$ under full-domain verification when the target expansion length is $1$ and extends to larger expansion lengths under suffix-only verification. Second, we refute the claimed ideal RUP integrity bound for variable-expansion online authenticated encryption. Even with an ideal tweakable online permutation, prior unverified decryption queries at smaller expansion lengths can reveal part of the target authentication suffix. We construct counterexamples showing that two such decryption queries and one forgery attempt achieve a success probability of $3/8$, exceeding the claimed bound of $1/4$. We also derive a general expression for the forgery success probability. Finally, we discuss the corresponding repairing

item.title: Threshold Batched Attribute-Based Encryption from Succinct LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2822
Authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal
Summary: Batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) enables a single compact key to decrypt ciphertexts associated with a designated batch of identities. Batched attribute-based encryption (B-ABE) extends this functionality to attribute-based access control, while threshold batched attribute-based encryption (TB-ABE) further distributes the decryption capability among multiple parties. Existing constructions of TB-ABE rely on bilinear pairings, motivating post-quantum alternatives. In this work, we give, to the best of our knowledge, the first lattice-based candidate construction of TB-ABE. Our construction combines the succinct polynomial-digest mechanism underlying lattice-based BIBE with key-homomorphic evaluation for arithmetic-circuit policies and linear secret sharing. We prove security under the ℓ-succinct LWE assumption, assuming the required share-uniformity property of the underlying ramp threshold sharing scheme.

item.title: Designing Quantum-Safe Network Architectures via Certified Randomness Distribution
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2821
Authors: Filip-Ioan Ceară, Diana Maimuţ
Summary: We propose an alternative design for quantum-safe network architectures, based on distributing certified randomness generated by different trust-level QRNGs. Our modular methodology aggregates high-trust entropy from upper network layers with local contributions, enhancing the security guarantees of locally available random sequences. Leveraging the physical guarantees of QRNGs and symmetric-key cryptographic algorithms for node authentication, our approach enables immediately deployable, quantum-safe infrastructures. Such a paradigm bypasses the practical security limitations of current QKD-based solutions, while avoiding massive key sizes and latency inherent to asymmetric PQC implementations.

item.title: The Minimum Bucket Capacity for Reliable Path ORAM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2820
Authors: Yijia Chang, Man Ho Au
Summary: Path ORAM hides memory access patterns by storing $N$ data blocks in a binary tree whose buckets have capacity $Z$, using a client-side stash for blocks that cannot be placed in the tree. Smaller buckets reduce storage and communication costs but increase the risk of stash overflow. The revised Path ORAM analysis in 2014 established an exponentially decreasing stash overflow probability for $Z \geq 5$. Experiments suggest small stashes at $Z=4$ and substantially larger ones at $Z=3$. However, it remained unknown whether $Z=4$ admits a uniform exponential stash bound or whether such a bound is impossible at $Z=3$.
We establish a sharp threshold at $Z=4$ for binary Path ORAM with tree depth $L=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$. For $Z=4$, we prove that, uniformly over all database sizes and fixed access sequences, the stash size $S$ after the final refill satisfies \[ \Pr[S>R] \leq \frac{23}{28}\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^R \] for every integer $R \geq 0$. For $Z=3$, we exhibit a family of instances on which a single sequential scan of all $N$ blocks produces a stash of size $\Omega(N)$ with probability bounded away from zero. Thus, four is the minimum bucket capacity admitting a uniform exponential stash bound: a logarithmic stash suffices for polynomial-length executions with inverse-polynomial failure probability at $Z=4$, whereas at $Z=3$ no sublinear stash can make the overflow probability vanish uniformly.
Our proofs connect the actual Path ORAM process with dependent node loads to an auxiliary model with independent geometric node loads. This independence enables a recursive analysis of overflow that avoids the union bound over rooted subtrees used in the previous $Z=5$ proof. The main challenge is to transfer bounds from the auxiliary model to the actual process, which requires different techniques for the upper and lower bounds. For $Z=4$, we develop a two-stage randomization argument that bounds the actual process's exponential overflow moment by that of the auxiliary model. For $Z=3$, we develop a local continuous-time approximation with controlled errors that transfers an overflow surplus from the auxiliary model to the actual process, yielding the linear stash lower bound. Together, these arguments establish the sharp threshold at bucket capacity four.

item.title: How to Revoke Users in Encryption Schemes?
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2819
Authors: Sanjam Garg, Dimitris Kolonelos, Benjamin Ostrovsky, Guru-Vamsi Policharla
Summary: Revocation is essential for keeping encryption secure as keys leak, devices are compromised or users leave the system. We revisit the problem of revocation for encryption schemes and give, to our knowledge, the first approach combining anonymous, collusion-resistant revocation with unchanged keys and access rules, succinct ciphertext overhead and a trustless revocation authority, i.e. that cannot decrypt. Revoking a user publishes one random-looking pseudonym, without telling encryptors whose key was revoked. A party can decrypt future ciphertexts only if it is unrevoked and satisfies the original access decryption rule.
Our core observation is that revocation is, at heart, witness encryption for the statement that one satisfies the access rule and that the pseudonym bound to one's key has not been revoked. Although general-purpose witness encryption remains far from practical, we observe that the statements arising from revocation are simple and algebraic, and we show that they fall within the special-purpose framework of Garg et al. (CRYPTO 2025), which compiles short arguments of knowledge (called ``gadgets'') into efficient witness encryption using bilinear groups. Our technical contribution is a pair of succinct non-membership gadgets for this framework, one for a single hidden pseudonym and one that certifies non-revocation jointly for all users selected by an access rule. Both gadgets are generic and modular, as they compose with the gadgets expressing a wide range of access rules, and thus provide a single revocation mechanism that is designed once and reused across different encryption schemes, without redesigning either the scheme or the revocation.
These gadgets yield the following applications. First, we give a black-box transformation adding revocation to arbitrary independently instantiated public-key encryption, with constant-size cryptographic ciphertext overhead. For unrevoked users, confidentiality continues to rely only on the security of the underlying scheme. Then, we demonstrate applications to advanced encryption scheme, constructing revocable schemes for distributed broadcast, registered attribute-based, and registered threshold encryption, with succinct cryptographic ciphertext components and threshold decryption shares. We prove adaptive security of our schemes in the generic bilinear-group and random-oracle models.

item.title: Round-Optimal Statistical Verifiable Secret Sharing with Polynomial Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2818
Authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova
Summary: Verifiable secret sharing (Chor, Goldwasser, Micali, and Awerbuch; FOCS'85) is a central primitive in secure computation, and its round complexity has been studied extensively.
Rabin and Ben-Or [STOC'89] established the feasibility of statistical security up to $t2$ corruptions, and Patra, Choudhary, Rabin, and Rangan [Crypto'09] showed that three sharing rounds are necessary. The work of Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra [STOC'23] introduced the first round-optimal VSS with three rounds of sharing and one round for reconstruction, albeit with exponential communication in the number of parties.
We give the first round-optimal statistical VSS that has polynomial communication and computation for $t2$. This resolves the efficiency question left open by Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra. The protocol is obtained from a new notion of weak secret sharing, in which the reconstruction-time freedom of a corrupt dealer is limited to choosing verification keys, which is of independent interest.

item.title: From Degree Three to Degree Two: Statistical Randomized Encodings for All Functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2817
Authors: Emmanuela Orsini, Arpita Patra
Summary: A randomized encoding represents a function by a simpler randomized map whose output allows recovery of the function value while revealing essentially no further information about the input. Perfectly correct and perfectly private encodings of degree three over $\F_2$ are known for every Boolean function, but degree two cannot provide these guarantees for all functions (Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2000 and ICALP 2002). Whether degree two suffices when small statistical errors are allowed in both correctness and privacy has remained open.
We construct quadratic randomized encodings of every Boolean function with exponentially small correctness and statistical privacy errors. The degree bound holds jointly in the input bits and independent uniform random bits, and the construction, encoder, decoder and simulator have complexity polynomial in the total size of mod-2 branching programs computing the function's output bits and in the security parameter. Our encodings also achieve decomposability and output locality three, meaning that each encoded bit depends on at most three input and random bits. These results resolve the degree-two and locality-three questions for statistical randomized encodings (Ishai, 2013). As an application, we obtain one-way functions of optimal output locality three from one-way functions in polynomial-time uniform $\mathrm{NC}^1$, improving the previous locality-four result under the same assumption (Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2004).
We also obtain quadratic multiparty randomized encodings with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against semi-honest corruption of any coalition of parties. Previous general constructions for $k\ge4$ parties provided perfect correctness and privacy against at most $\lfloor 2k/3\rfloor$ corruptions (Applebaum, Ishai, Karni and Patra, CRYPTO 2022). Through known reductions, our encodings yield non-interactive reductions of every functionality to a fixed three-party functionality and three-round protocols in the two-round OT-hybrid model, with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against every coalition. They also yield non-interactive client--server protocols for every function whenever a majority of the servers is honest, even when corrupted servers collude with any set of clients. This server threshold is optimal in this model when privacy is required against arbitrary client coalitions.

item.title: SoK: Understanding Virtual Machines over Fully Homomorphic Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2816
Authors: Song Bian, Ziwei Ma, Yunhao Fu, Haowen Pan, Ruiyu Shen, Zhou Zhang, Ran Mao, Zaidong Li, Yintai Sun, Ruoyi Li, Zhenyu Guan
Summary: We survey the current literature on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) from a virtual machine (VM) perspective. We observe that programs behave in an intrinsically different way over FHE than on plaintext, forming a new paradigm of computation that is fundamentally constrained by the obliviousness of data. To better understand the computational properties, we compile more than 125 works to formulate a cross-layer systematic view of FHE VMs, with a special focus on understanding the concrete programming models over encrypted data. In particular, we identify three distinct forms of VMs over FHE, namely, the SISD VM, the SIMD VM, and the hybrid VM. To aid the cross-layer systematization, we also discuss how current FHE compilers and hardware accelerators can be applied to enhance the usability and performance of the respective VMs. In the experiment, we test eight VM instructions with varying precision as well as two end-to-end application programs to quantitatively assess the concrete design trade-offs for each of the VM paradigms. We conclude that FHE VMs of different types exhibit distinct utility and performance characteristics, necessitating new design methodologies to be developed in a cross-layer manner.

item.title: Jazzline: Composable CryptoLine Functional Correctness Proofs for Jasmin Programs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2815
Authors: José Bacelar Almeida, Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Lionel Blatter, Gustavo Delerue, João Diogo Duarte, Benjamin Gregoire, Tiago Oliveira, Miguel Quaresma, Pierre-Yves Strub, Ming-Hsien Tsai, Bow-Yaw Wang, Bo-Yin Yang
Summary: Jasmin is a programming language for high-speed and high-assurance cryptography. Correctness proofs of Jasmin programs are typically carried out deductively in EasyCrypt. This allows generality, modularity and composable reasoning, but does not scale well for low-level architecture-specific routines. CryptoLine offers a semi-automatic approach to formally verify algebraically-rich low-level cryptographic routines. CryptoLine proofs are self-contained: they are not integrated into higher-level formal verification developments. This paper shows how to soundly use CryptoLine to discharge subgoals in functional correctness proofs for complex Jasmin programs. We extend Jasmin with annotations and provide an automatic translation into a CryptoLine model, where most complex transformations are certified. We also formalize and implement the automatic extraction of the semantics of a CryptoLine proof

item.title: Registration-based Encryption with Logarithmic Registration
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2814
Authors: Xingfu Yan, Guiqiu Liao, Fan Yang, Haining Yang, Zheng Gong, Fucai Luo, Bowen Zhao
Summary: Registration-based encryption (RBE) preserves IBE's identity-only encryption interface while eliminating key escrow: users generate their own keys, and a Key Curator manages only registered public keys. However, this design introduces a new challenge: user registration, since every joining user rrequires KC to update the registry. Although theoretical RBE constructions achieve polylogarithmic registration, they rely on costly cryptographic techniques and remain impractical. In existing deployable black-box RBE, registration takes $O(\sqrt{N})$ time ($N$ denotes the maximum user capacity). This gap between theoretical registration efficiency and deployability makes registration a key performance bottleneck for large-scale deployments of pairing-based RBE.
This work presents a black-box pairing-based RBE construction under the decisional $(R,S,T,f)$-Diffie-Hellman assumption. Build on the multilinear tree, when registering a user's public key, KC updates only the corresponding root-to-leaf path associated with the user. Therefore, registration in our construction takes $O(\log \sqrt{N})$ time for the maximum user capacity $N$. Moreover, we provides membership and non-membership verification, and their batch verification supports to check registration status of multiple users. Experiments show registration and key generation complete in milliseconds when $N=10^7$. Compared with Glaeser et al. (CCS'23), our scheme accelerates registration by up to \(158\times\) and key generation by up to \(230\times\) with practical overheads.

item.title: Overcoming Padding in Cryptography via Hardness of Certifying Random Strings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2813
Authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh, Abhishek Jain, Jiatu Li, Surya Mathialagan
Summary: Modern cryptography relies on a provable security paradigm where the security of a primitive is established from the intractability of one or more computational problems. Hybrid arguments are central to this approach. Somewhat unexpectedly, many security proofs in the literature that use this methodology require hybrids with description-size larger than the real scheme. To argue security, the real scheme is artificially padded to match this size. This so-called “superfluous padding” phenomenon is surprisingly commonplace and poses a barrier to achieving succinct cryptographic primitives where the size of the scheme parameters does not grow with the input length.
We present a framework to eliminate padding in cryptography. We demonstrate several applications, including rate-1 iO, succinct (and extractable) witness encryption and succinct non-interactive arguments with short CRS for subclasses of NP, and multi-input functional encryption for functions with unbounded arity.
To obtain our results, we establish a new connection between cryptography and proof complexity. Central to our approach is the notion of proof-complexity generators (PCGs) [Krajíček'01, Alekhnovich, Ben-Sasson, Razborov, Wigderson'04], which, informally speaking, formalizes the hardness of certifying random (incompressible) strings with propositional proof systems. Our applications are derived from a master theorem that lifts cryptographic security on “compressible instances” to security on any instance under the existence of PCGs. Due to its broad scope, this theorem might find future application

item.title: Constructions of Boolean Correctors with Optimal Nonlinearity and Vectorial Correctors Beyond Optimal Linear Correction Order
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2812
Authors: Zhaole Li, Deng Tang
Summary: Correctors are postprocessing functions that reduce or eliminate statistical bias in raw bitstreams produced by physical noise sources in true random number generators. In this paper, we develop a framework based on binary Krawtchouk polynomials for analyzing and constructing Boolean and vectorial correctors. This framework reformulates the Walsh-layer criterion into finite moment constraints on support-layer counts and preimage-layer counts. We also establish universal upper bounds on the nonlinearity of correctors, and necessary conditions on the achievable correction order. For Boolean functions, we prove that $(n-1)$-correctors are either the parity function or its complement. Then we characterize the support-layer profiles of $(n-2)$- and $(n-3)$-correctors and establish upper bounds on nonlinearity. For $n=2^k\ge 8$, a self-addressing construction yields $(n-2)$-correctors achieving the optimal nonlinearity $2^{n-1}-2^{n-1}/n$ with resiliency $n/2-2$ and algebraic degree $k+1$. Notably, this provides the first known infinite family of nonlinear correctors achieving both optimal correction order and optimal nonlinearity for that order, while having a resiliency strictly lower than the correction order. Furthermore, using constant-weight addressing, we construct $(n-d-1)$-correctors that asymptotically meet the nonlinearity upper bounds for every fixed $d\ge 1$. Our profile characterization also reveals inherent limitations of injective Maiorana--McFarland constructions at correction order $n-3$. For vectorial functions, we construct nonlinear $(s(2^m-1),m,s2^{m-1}+\ell-1)$-correctors for every $m\ge 2$ under certain conditions on $s$ and $\ell$, with resiliency at most $s2^{m-1}-2$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first infinite family of nonlinear correctors whose correction order simultaneously exceeds that of optimal linear corrector and its own resiliency. Finally, we introduce a secondary construction that lifts these vectorial correctors to larger input dimensions while preserving their correction-order advantage. This approach yields a nonlinearity of $2^{n-1}-2^{n-n_0-1}$, where $n_0$ is the input dimension of the base corrector, along with explicit resiliency and a flexible algebraic degree.

item.title: More Keys, Less Commitment: Key-Committing Attacks on BBB Accordions via Encode-then-Encipher and a Key-Committing Transform
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2811
Authors: Donghoon Chang, Yukihito Hiraga, Yusuke Naito, Yu Sasaki, Takeshi Sugawara
Summary: Cryptographic accordions with beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security are being actively studied in connection with NIST’s ongoing standardization effort. We show that BBB security of an accordion does not necessarily strengthen key commitment of AE built from it: in many BBB accordions, additional keys introduced for BBB security give an adversary extra degrees of freedom. Exploiting this observation, we present $O(1)$ key-committing attacks on a broad range of AE schemes built from BBB accordions, mostly via the Encode-then-Encipher (EtE) paradigm, including CHCTR2, eCTR-based accordions, THCTR, HCTR+, TCT2, and bbb-ddd-AES under a natural polynomial-hash instantiation. To address this issue, we propose CACH, a black-box transform from BBB-secure accordions to robust AE (RAE) with key-committing security. CACH achieves BBB multi-user RAE security and achieves $t/2$-bit key-committing security with a $t$-bit tag for $n \le t \le 2n$ in the ideal-cipher model. CACH uses only AES-based components and supports all AES key sizes, making it compatible with NIST’s design goals. We instantiate CACH with CHCTR2. CACH-CHCTR2 with AES-256 outperforms EtE-HCTR2 with Rijndael-256 and EtE-CHCTR2 for short messages.

item.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2810
Authors: Maksym Ioffe, Dahlia Malkhi
Summary: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. Designed for quorum-based systems, QUASI enables parties to attest to external entities that the statement is valid. Surprisingly, each party need not sign the entire statement: authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for the quorum to attest to the whole. A simple deterministic construction illustrates this possibility. Built purely from hashing and error correction, QUASI achieves small per-party contributions and low attestation generation and verification costs, without relying on SNARKs for aggregation.
Our main contribution is a randomized construction achieving reductions of more than $10\times$ in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures.
QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

item.title: Pastel: Single Secret Leader Election with Private Weights
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2809
Authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Kevin Choi, Intak Hwang, Jaehee Kang, Alireza Kavousi, Junho Lee, Yongdong Yeo
Summary: A single secret leader election (SSLE) protocol allows an election of exactly one leader among $n$ parties in a secrecy-preserving manner, where only the elected leader knows it has won until it publicly announces and claims leadership. Motivated by proof-of-stake blockchains where stakes are stored in an encrypted or committed form for the sake of privacy, we design and implement the first SSLE protocol with private weights. Each party's probability of winning an election in our protocol is weighted by stake, and these weights are private. Prior schemes in the literature only allow probabilistic (i.e. expectation of one but can be zero or many leaders) elections in the same setting.
Preserving privacy also means public verification is paramount in order for a protocol to be practically reliable. In this respect, our protocol achieves security against malicious adversaries with a concrete implementation. In particular, we concretely implement the needed zero-knowledge proofs and thus do not rely on slashing (financial penalties) to achieve end-to-end malicious security, though slashing can still serve as a performance optimization. Along the way, we observe that previous SSLE protocols in a setting without private weights (either unweighted or with public weights) are either maliciously secure with implementation or post-quantum secure but not both, while our protocol achieves both.

item.title: An improved algorithm to solve the isogeny problem in dimension 2 with precomputation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2808
Authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos
Summary: We give a new algorithm for the superspecial isogeny problem in dimension $2$. After a one-time precomputation depending only on $p$ (which succeeds with overwhelming probability), each instance is solved in expected time and memory $p^{3/4+o(1)}$. This result is unconditional, relying on no heuristics. Including the precomputation, a single instance is solved in time $p^{19/23+o(1)}$, improving on the $p^{1+o(1)}$ of the Costello-Smith algorithm. The improvement holds even with the same memory as (the rigorous version of) their algorithm.
The key ingredient is an algorithm that computes the equations of the Humbert surfaces $\mathcal{H}_{N^2}$ modulo $p$ for all $N$ up to a bound $D$ growing with $p$. These equations give a membership test for optimally $(N,N)$-split surfaces, which we evaluate in batches using fast multipoint evaluation. This speeds up the bottleneck of the Costello-Smith algorithm: finding an isogeny from a superspecial principally polarised abelian surface to a product of supersingular elliptic curves.

item.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2807
Authors: William Diamond, Fatima Elsheimy, Dahlia Malkhi, Geoff Ramseyer, Srivatsan Sridhar
Summary: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer.
We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering.
The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

item.title: On Proximity Gaps for Expander Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2806
Authors: Kobi Gurkan, Andrija Novakovic, Ron D. Rothblum
Summary: Proximity gaps describe a phenomenon concerning random linear combinations of words and their distance from a linear error-correcting code. Informally, they address the following question: if a collection of words is jointly far from the code, is a random linear combination of those words likely to also remain far from the code?
Motivated by applications to concretely efficient proof systems, in this note we study this question for expander codes, a class of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Recent works of Goyal and Guruswami (STOC 2026) and Goyal, Guruswami, Sun, and Wootters (RANDOM 2026; arXiv 2026) establish proximity gaps approaching capacity for random LDPC ensembles, but only asymptotically and for very large degrees and field sizes, well beyond what is used in practical proof systems.
We focus on general expander codes (not necessarily random) with small degree. Building on the smoothness property of expander codes due to Dinur, Sudan, and Wigderson (RANDOM 2006), we show that such codes have proximity gaps up to nearly half of the distance guaranteed by their expansion.

item.title: SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-box Reductions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2805
Authors: Zhengzhong Jin, Mingqi Lu, Bo Peng
Summary: We construct the first succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) from the polynomial-hardness of Learning with Errors (LWE) for a subclass of UP languages whose witness unambiguity has a polynomial-size Extended Frege ($\mathcal{EF}$) proof. Our construction achieves the following soundness guarantee:
For any fixed sequence of false instances $\{x_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$, there exists a (non-constructive) constant $c>0$ such that, whenever the uniform random CRS length exceeds $\lambda^c$, the construction achieves infinitely-often soundness for this sequence $\{x_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$: for any polynomial-time cheating prover $\{\mathcal{A}_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{N}}$, the probability that $\mathcal{A}_\lambda$ outputs an accepting proof for $x_\lambda$ is negligible for infinitely many $\lambda$.
As intermediate results, we also obtain: - SNARGs for any NP language that has polynomial-size $\mathcal{EF}$ proofs of witness unambiguity for all instances outside of the language, based on polynomial-hard LWE, achieving the same style of soundness guarantee. - SNARKs for all true instances in any language $L \in \mathsf{UP}$ where every instance has a polynomial-size $\mathcal{EF}$ proof of witness unambiguity, under polynomial hardness of LWE, without soundness guarantees for false instances.
To achieve our main result, we employ a non-black-box soundness reduction. Along the way, we introduce a new logical proof system, the \emph{Cryptographic Extended Frege} ($\mathcal{CEF}$) system, which extends $\mathcal{EF}$ with rules for formalizing the indistinguishability in cryptographic security proofs. Building on the Encrypt-hash-and-BARG framework of [Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan, STOC’24], we further obtain SNARGs for NP languages that have $\mathcal{CEF}$ proofs of non-membership, which may be of independent interest.

item.title: Actively Secure PIR from Verifiable Linear Relations over Rings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2804
Authors: Louis Tremblay Thibault
Summary: Privately retrieving data from a database without revealing which element is being retrieved is a fundamental problem in cryptography with many diverse applications. State-of-the-art solutions to this problem are generally based on homomorphic encryption, which offers security only against passive adversaries. In this work, we contribute to the recently introduced notion of Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR), which leverages verifiable computation to achieve security against active adversaries. We present a new sum-check based interactive oracle proof for linear relations over power-of-two cyclotomic rings, and show how to instantiate it into a vPIR protocol using Ring-LWE. Our solution is concretely efficient, offers the best possible security guarantees and is plausibly post-quantum secure. We additionally provide an open-source Rust implementation. Our server time improves on prior work's IOP by more than an order of magnitude, leading to a factor two end-to-end performance improvement. Compared to vPIR prior work, on a 4 GiB database, our offline communication and client storage are of 128 MiB, against 3.29 GiB. Preprocessing is run once per database and amortized over an unbounded number of queries.

item.title: The GGM PRF Construction is Optimal
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2803
Authors: Bar Alon, Itai Dinur, Muthuramakrishnan Venkitasubramaniam
Summary: We study the complexity of fully black-box constructions of pseudorandom functions (PRFs) from pseudorandom generators (PRGs). The seminal work of Goldreich, Goldwasser, and Micali (JACM 1986), combined with Levin’s domain-extension technique, yields PRFs that make a superlogarithmic number of adaptive calls to a length-doubling PRG. A long-standing open problem is whether fewer calls suffice for fully black-box constructions. Despite progress for restricted classes of constructions and reductions, previous results have not been able to rule out even a single-call construction in full generality. A related question asks how many calls are needed to amplify a PRG’s stretch from \(r\) bits to \(\rho>r\) bits.
Our main result establishes the asymptotic optimality of the GGM construction with domain compression, both in the number of calls and in adaptivity, for length-doubling PRGs. More generally, for a PRG with seed length \(n\) and stretch \(r(n)\), we rule out fully black-box PRF constructions with \(d(n)\) adaptive rounds whenever \(d(n)\log(2+r(n)/n)=O(\log n)\), even allowing polynomially many calls per round. Our bounds hold for one-bit weak PRFs on domains of superpolynomial size. In particular, they exclude all polynomial-query nonadaptive constructions from PRGs of arbitrary polynomial stretch and require superlogarithmically many rounds when the underlying PRG doubles its input length.
We further show impossibility results for fully black-box non-adaptive PRG stretch amplification. First, we show that a non-adaptive construction of a $\rho$-bit stretch PRG from an $r$-bit stretch PRG requires $\Omega(\tfrac{\rho}{r+\log n})$ calls. Second, we show that it is impossible to construct a length-doubling PRG from an $o(n)$-bit stretch PRG with non-adaptive calls.
Our techniques combine and extend two prior lines of work. First, we develop a sensitivity framework that measures the effect of changing a uniformly chosen oracle entry and transfers this stability through black-box reductions, extending the sensitivity arguments of Bitansky et al. (CRYPTO 2017) and Bitansky and Degwekar (TCC 2019). Second, we extend the scoring mechanism of Alon et al. (CRYPTO 2026) and integrate it with our framework. Finally, we show that the sensitivity framework applies to constructions from one-way permutations. Specifically, we show another proof of Simon's impossibility of basing collision-resistant hash functions on one-way permutations. Our new proof can be viewed as an abstraction of the argument by Bitansky and Degwekar.

item.title: Filtered merges make deeper representation trees pay: Subset Sum and Meet-LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2802
Authors: Nick Howgrave-Graham
Summary: Dubiner's bucketing codes, used as type-class filters on representation coordinates, let a merge avoid generating matched pairs with the wrong split pattern. We show that in representation trees their main effect is to make depth pay. For random density-one Subset Sum they improve the exponent of Bonnetain, Bricout, Schrottenloher and Shen from 0.2831 (our recomputation) to 0.2690, at depth 5; no better point was found up to depth 9. For May's Meet-LWE on ternary keys they improve the asymptotic exponent by 0.013–0.023 for key weights ω ≥ 0.375. Filters can pay only at merges where most matched pairs have the wrong split pattern, and do pay where such merges bind; we show both where this holds and where it fails. A survival recursion justifies the accounting, a symmetry lemma shows that the filters cannot bias the planted solution, and simulations support the remaining heuristics.

item.title: Parallelizable modes for duplex-based authenticated encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2801
Authors: Joan Daemen, Silvia Mella, Gilles Van Assche
Summary: This note enriches the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE-based authenticated encryption schemes defined by Daemen et al. at EuroS&P 2025 with parallelizable ones, while keeping their security properties. The main contribution is a new deck cipher mode, called FlightDeck, that has the ability of processing input strings similarly to KangarooTwelve and producing output strings as in counter mode, so both parallelizable. We then instantiate FlightDeck on top of the overwrite duplex (OD) construction, in turn on top of a Keccak-p permutation. Combined with a deck cipher-based mode like Deck-BO, the security of the resulting authenticated encryption schemes reduces to the PRF security of keyed (Turbo)SHAKE and to the collision resistance of (Turbo)SHAKE. Compared to the schemes defined at EuroS&P 2025, replacing UpperDeck with FlightDeck greatly improves their software efficiency as one can implement them with Keccak-p permutations evaluated in parallel.

item.title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2800
Authors: Emanuele Bellini
Summary: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which Göloğlu and Pavlů proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certificates. No function in these classes or in their switching closure is CCZ-equivalent to a permutation. All code and data are public.

item.title: Exploring the Set of APN Functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2799
Authors: Jules Baudrin, Pierre Galissant, Léo Perrin
Summary: An Almost Perfect Nonlinear (APN) function $F : \mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2^n$ provides optimal protection against differential attacks, meaning that the equation $F(x+a)=F(x)+b$ has at most 2 solutions~$x$ when $a \neq 0$. Setting aside some sporadic examples, such functions are hard to find in practice, and whether there exists APN bijections of $ \mathbb{F}_2^n$ when $n > 6$ is even (the Big APN Problem) is still unknown.
In this paper, we provide the tools needed to explore the complete set of known APN functions. Indeed, for a given APN function $F$, we in fact know many: all functions CCZ-equivalent to $F$ are also APN, and so are its switching neighbours. These notions have been in the literature for many years, but several unknowns remain that complicate the exploration of the corresponding functions in practice: a given function has too many switching neighbours, and the algorithms that are known to iterate through a CCZ-equivalence class return multiple representatives per extended-affine (EA) equivalence class.
We solve both problems. First, we show how to partition precisely the CCZ-equivalence class of a quadratic APN function in practice, and thus obtain exactly one representative per EA-equivalence class. To achieve this, we carefully investigate the set of the automorphisms of the graph of a quadratic APN function, and show how to generate them very efficiently using the ortho-derivative. Second, we provide the first detailed investigation of the set of the switching neighbours of a function, show in particular how an overwhelming majority of them are trivial, and explain how to get rid of those. Incidentally, we build a new extended-affine equivalence class invariant using the resulting set of non-trivial switching neighbours.
For both theoretical contributions, we pushed highly-efficient and easy to re-use implementations of the corresponding algorithms to the sboxU library. It allowed us to generate databases containing all known APN functions for $n=6$ and $n=7$. For $n=8$, our algorithms are efficient-enough that we can investigate the properties of the millions of quadratic APN function recently exhibited. In the process, we generate a few thousands of new CCZ-equivalence classes.
In the light of our work, the successes of the exploration strategies for $n=6$ (i.e. finding an APN function inequivalent to any monomial and quadratic mapping, and finding an APN bijection in even dimension) seems to be an artifact due to the small dimension that we show not to work for dimension 8 and which we do not expect to work either when the dimension is greater.

item.title: More Salt, Please: A Simple Compiler for Post-Quantum Strong aPAKE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2798
Authors: William Riccardo Duro, Sebastian Faller, Julia Hesse, Máté Horváth
Summary: Resistance to precomputation attacks is a central security goal in password-based cryptography, as it drastically increases the runtime of brute-force attacks on breached password hashes. Strong asymmetric password-authenticated key exchange (saPAKE), which enforces such precomputation resistance, is standardized by the IRTF and deployed today at large scale. Unfortunately, no practical and easy-to-deploy saPAKE exists yet that withstands quantum attackers. Current constructions use rate-limiting tools such as oblivious pseudo-random functions (OPRFs), of which post-quantum versions are significantly more costly and complex than their discrete-log based counterparts.
In this paper, we take a new approach to precomputation resistance. Starting from the compilers from PAKE to aPAKE by Gentry-MacKenzie-Ramzan (Crypto 2006) and Liu-Lyu-Han (Asiacrypt 2024), we propose a password file ratchet that adds precomputation resistance to these compilers through continuously updating the password file. The update is a simple salted hash. With a variety of practical post-quantum PAKEs at hand, this yields a ready-to-deploy post-quantum saPAKE at the trade-off of a changing server state.

item.title: The Maximum Possible Nonlinearity for a Balanced Boolean Function in 10 Variables is 492
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2797
Authors: Youle Xu, Qichun Wang
Summary: Determining the maximum nonlinearity of 10-variable balanced Boolean functions has been a long-standing open problem. In this paper, we resolve it by proving that the maximum nonlinearity is exactly 492, thereby confirming Dobbertin’s conjecture in dimension 10. To exclude nonlinearity 494, we derive a quadratic residue for the Walsh spectrum and refine a local energy table from four-block concatenation by retaining the signs of the Walsh coefficients. The resulting bounds exclude all but the largest polar rank; a product inequality and a parity argument eliminate the remaining case.

item.title: Applying Combinatorial Techniques To Find Minimal Non-Complete Set Coverings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2796
Authors: Enrico Piccione, Jan Vorloeper
Summary: One of the most prominent hardware countermeasures against side-channel attacks are threshold implementations (TIs). The technique uses masking to split the operations in a cryptographic algorithm into several ones operating on shares. The coverage and non-completeness requirements of TIs are mathematically described by the notion of non-complete set coverings (NCSCs). Importantly, the number of members inside an NCSC determines the number of output shares and therefore directly impacts the complexity of the resulting TI.
In this work, we derive new lower bounds on the minimal number of members of NCSCs and obtain new upper bounds by explicit constructions. We present a group-theoretic construction of balanced NCSCs, in which the numbers of input and output shares coincide, together with a search algorithm based on intersections of group translates. Our methods determine the smallest balanced coverings in two previously unresolved cases and yield exact minima and classifications of optimal coverings for an infinite family of parameters. These results resolve all four explicit open problems posed by Farr\`as, Fidalgo and Lara-Nino.

item.title: Exploiting Matrix-Vector Multiplication in AIMer: Single-Trace Attacks on Key Generation and Signing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2795
Authors: Süleyman Emir Akın, Abdullah Talayhan, Özcan Öztürk
Summary: This paper presents two side-channel attacks against AIMer v3.0, one of the two signature schemes selected in the Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography (KpqC) competition. Both are single-trace attacks that recover the full secret key without a profiling phase, one against key generation and one against signing. Both target the same routine: the matrix-vector multiplication invoked by either phase expands each bit of its secret operand into an all-zero or an all-one mask, which then gates the accumulation of the corresponding public matrix row. A single execution therefore leaks one distinguishable segment per secret bit. What makes the attacks non-profiled is that each attacked trace carries its own labelled training set. During key generation, creating the dense invertible public matrices invokes the matrix-vector multiplication routine hundreds of times, on operands that are public. In signing the same derivation takes place, and in addition the signature itself opens all but one of the $N$ parties of every repetition, so the bits of nearly every multiplication in the trace are public. In both attacks we use a supervised classifier to recover the unknown value. In key generation that value is the private key itself, whereas in signing there are three distinct routes to it: the key itself, a party's share of the key, and a party's share of an S-box output. Recovering any one of them is enough to recover the private key. We validate both attacks on an ARM Cortex-M4: one trace recovers the exact secret key from every capture we took, $100$ key generations for each of AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, and $100$ signatures for each of AES-128f, AES-192f and AES-256f. We also discuss possible countermeasures.

item.title: BeaverDam: A Post-Quantum Threshold Key Recovery Protocol from a One-Time Threshold Oblivious Random Function
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2794
Authors: Benedikt Auerbach, Shuichi Katsumata, Kaoru Takemure, Ida Tucker
Summary: Secure backups are a practical necessity of E2EE messaging apps, typically relying on password-protected key-recovery (PPKR) protocols. These allow users to turn a human-memorable password into a cryptographic key with the help of a server. Recently, Signal and Juicebox proposed threshold PPKR (tPPKR) protocols, removing the trust on a centralized server. Unfortunately, known solutions are only classically secure, lagging behind the shift toward post-quantum (PQ), or to be more precise, hybrid secure E2EE.
We present BeaverDam, a novel tPPKR protocol that is PQ secure with efficiency close to existing classical protocols. It also easily extends to hybrid security, standing as the first concretely efficient hybrid-secure tPPKR protocol. BeaverDam relies on a new primitive we introduce --- one-time threshold oblivious random functions (tORF). Unlike full-fledged OPRFs, which are notoriously difficult to construct in a PQ-secure manner, one-time tORF offers weaker but sufficient security guarantees tailored to the tPPKR setting.
We then construct an efficient one-time tORF called Beaver, inspired by multi-party computation (MPC) techniques. Owing to the one-time feature, we only need to securely compute a 2-wise independent hash function, making our protocol very efficient. We conclude by presenting a practical instantiation of BeaverDam and comparing its performance to state-of-the-art classical tPPKR protocols, namely Signal's SVR3 and Juicebox.

item.title: Weights Come Almost for Free in Ramp Threshold Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2793
Authors: Aarushi Goel, Mingyuan Wang
Summary: A weighted threshold access structure assigns a weight to each party and authorizes a subset of parties whenever their total weight exceeds a prescribed threshold. Most existing approaches to designing multiparty cryptographic protocols in the weighted threshold setting, however, either incur complexity that grows with the total weight assigned to the parties or remain far from concretely efficient.
Toward \emph{concretely efficient} weighted threshold primitives, we take a different route and relax to the \emph{ramp} setting, in which two thresholds are prescribed: a subset whose total weight falls below an $\alpha$ fraction of the total is unauthorized, while a subset whose total weight exceeds a $\beta$ fraction is authorized. Exploiting the gap between these two thresholds, we obtain the following results.
1. Given any weighted ramp threshold access structure with privacy threshold $\alpha$ and reconstruction threshold $\beta$, where $0\!<\!\alpha\!<\!\beta\!<\!1$, we present a weight compression technique that reduces the total weight to $\approx n/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ while preserving the authorized and unauthorized sets. Combined with the standard player-virtualization paradigm, this yields concretely efficient weighted threshold cryptographic protocols with only a multiplicative overhead of $\approx 1/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ over their unweighted counterparts. Previously, the best known compression technique in this setting, due to Benhamouda et al.~[ITC'23], achieved total weight $\approx 5n/(\beta-\alpha)$.
2. Player virtualization has an inherent drawback: a party's share size and workload grow in proportion to its (compressed) weight, so the parties in which the most trust is placed also bear the largest computational and communication costs. Thus, although the \emph{overall} overhead is $O(1)$, the cost borne by a single party can still be $O(n)$ times that in the unweighted setting. Our second result removes this imbalance. Building on our compression technique, we construct a linear secret-sharing scheme in which every party receives a share of size $\widetilde{O}(1)$, independent of its weight, for a total share size of $\widetilde{O}(n)$, nearly matching the $O(n)$ complexity of standard unweighted threshold secret sharing.

item.title: Independent Leakage Does Not Save Evasive LWE: Refuting Folklore Fixes in the Private-Coin Setting
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2792
Authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh
Summary: The evasive learning with errors (evasive LWE) assumption has enabled a wide range of advanced cryptographic constructions from lattices in the past few years. The simple intuition that LWE remains secure even when additional ``non-zeroizing'' short preimages are given has proved highly versatile in applications. Unfortunately, recent counterexamples have refuted its general private-coin formulations, showing that having the short preimages along with arbitrary auxiliary leakage about the secret and target matrices can invalidate this intuition.
To preserve important applications, particularly witness encryption, the community has sought to repair the assumption by restricting the allowed leakage. One folklore proposal requires the secret and target matrices, together with their respective leakage, to be generated independently. This restriction appears to preserve the application to witness encryption while ruling out all previously known counterexamples.
In this work, we refute this proposal. Assuming LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation, we show that both the binding and hiding variants of private-coin evasive LWE are false even with the independent sampler restriction. Our counterexamples exploit only auxiliary leakage about the target matrix. We sample the secret honestly from a standard uniform or Gaussian distribution, independently of the target and its leakage, and we use no auxiliary information about the secret.

item.title: New Results in Adaptively-Secure Broadcast Encryption and Succinct Computational Secret Sharing from Standard Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2791
Authors: Rishab Goyal, Saikumar Yadugiri
Summary: Projective pseudorandom generators (PPRGs), introduced by [Applebaum et al.; STOC'23], expand a short seed into a long pseudorandom string, with a special feature that one can generate a short $\textit{projected}$ key, for any set $S$, such that it reveals the output bits in $S$ while preserving pseudorandomness of the remaining bits. They demonstrated that PPRGs can bypass the 'representation size barrier' in computational secret sharing schemes, and designed PPRGs assuming hardness of a variety of standard cryptographic assumptions. Later, [Hsieh, Waters, and Wu; EUROCRYPT'25] showed that PPRGs can also be used to design adaptively-secure broadcast encryption in the standard model, without relying on unprovable heuristics.
In this work, we design succinct computational secret sharing schemes for graph access structures and adaptively-secure flexible broadcast encryption in the standard model, both with optimal parameters. The main driver for both our results is a new construction of a compact programmable pseudorandom set sampler (PPS), introduced by [Goyal and Yadugiri; CRYPTO'26], from standard Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption [Regev; STOC'05]. We show that PPS generically imply PPRGs with many useful properties and, moreover, by replacing PPRGs with PPS we can achieve full succinctness in the underlying applications to secret sharing and adaptive security compilers for broadcast encryption. This yields the $\textit{first}$ flexible broadcast encryption scheme in the standard model from $\textit{any}$ falsifiable assumption with fully compact ciphertext size, and a succinct computational secret sharing for evolving graph access structures with optimal share size from standard LWE.

item.title: Vector Commit-and-Reduce Schemes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2790
Authors: Anubhav Baweja, Pratyush Mishra, Tushar Mopuri, Bharath Namboothiry
Summary: Hash-based argument systems are seeing increasing adoption in practice, owing to their ease of deployment, fast provers, and plausible post-quantum security. However, they still lag behind elliptic-curve counterparts due to their large proof sizes and (comparatively more) expensive verifiers. Attempts to optimize these metrics have focused on one of the two ingredients underlying these arguments, namely Interactive Oracle Reductions, leaving the other ingredient, Vector Commitments (VC) schemes largely ignored. This is in part because Merkle trees are the best known hash-based VC scheme to date.
To make progress on this front, we introduce Vector Commit-and-Reduce (VCR) schemes. These generalize VC schemes by allowing both the commitment and opening algorithms to be interactive protocols, and moreover by allowing the opening algorithm to be a reduction instead of an argument. By requiring VCR schemes to satisfy strong round-by-round knowledge soundness notions, we show how they can be used to construct hash-based reductions from IORs. Our transformation extends prior work which used (non-interactive) VC schemes.
We also provide a construction of a VCR scheme, Canopy, that greatly reduces proof size and verifier time by reducing the vector opening claims to proximity claims about certain (committed) codewords. This latter feature enables us to use a wide variety of techniques for proving, batching, and accumulating these claims, and indeed we use these to obtain both concrete and asymptotic improvements for hash-based arguments and reductions.
For SNARKs based on the Bolt code [CRYPTO 2026], we reduce proof sizes by 50\% and verifier hashes by $3\times$ with only a 5-15$\%$ prover overhead. For SNARKs based on the Reed-Solomon code, we reduce proof sizes by 20$\%$, and verifier hashes by $1.5\times$ with only a 20$\%$ prover overhead. We also construct hash-based Proof-Carrying Data where the recursion overhead is $O(\lambda \sqrt{\log N})$ hashes; in comparison, the state-of-the-art requires $\Omega(\lambda {\log N})$ hashes.

item.title: SETH: Subcode Equivalence in the Head
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2789
Authors: Marco Baldi, Michele Battagliola, Rahmi El Mechri, Laura Mattiuz, Marco Rinaudo, Paolo Santini, Riccardo Schiavoni, Edoardo Signorini
Summary: The Multi-Party Computation in the Head (MPCitH) paradigm has proven to be a versatile tool to design post-quantum digital signature schemes. Recently, MPCitH was improved with Threshold Computation in the Head (TCitH) and Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation in the Head (VOLEitH). In this paper, we propose two polynomial models for the Subcode Equivalence Problem (SEP) and derive TCitH and VOLEitH signatures from them. The resulting scheme has better performance when compared to other SEP-based signature schemes and also features shorter signatures when compared to other schemes based on similar assumptions.

item.title: Differentially Private Distance-Sensitive Representations for General Metrics
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2788
Authors: Paul Cesaretti
Summary: A distance-sensitive set representation stores a set $S$ from a metric space $(U,d)$ and answers queries of the form "is some element of $S$ within distance $r$ of $q$?''. Existing differentially private constructions are confined to Hamming space, because they route the query through a signature map built for that metric. We give a framework that removes this restriction. The released object records only the occupancy of a fixed public partition of $U$, so privacy transfers unchanged from an off-the-shelf private membership structure, and the entire metric dependence collapses into one packing quantity, the straddle number $\kappa$: the largest number of cells a ball of radius $r$ can meet. Any metric admitting a partition of width at most $(c-1)r$ and straddlenumber $\kappa$ then has an $\varepsilon$-differentially private $(c,r)$-representation with $\varepsilon =\ln(2\kappa/\alpha)$ in $O(k\log(\kappa/\alpha))$ bits.
Instantiating $\kappa$ gives matching upper and lower bounds in $\ell_\infty$ for partition-based constructions ($\varepsilon=O(\log d)$ at $c=\Theta(d)$, against $\varepsilon=\Omega(d)$ at constant $c$), and a randomized, dimension-free construction for every $\ell_p$ (one probe and $\varepsilon=\ln(2/\alpha)$ regardless of $d$) at the cost of a weaker, non-oblivious guarantee whose price is exactly this $\log d$ gap. For metrics available only through a distance oracle, we build the partition from a public net and a public navigable graph, and show that greedy search on that graph both locates and enumerates the cells a query must probe; on a $\lambda$-doubling metric this gives $\varepsilon\le 5\ln\lambda+\ln(2/\alpha)$. We further show that the per-query form of the guarantee is forced rather than chosen: any representation correct on all queries simultaneously requires $\varepsilon\ge\ln M+\ln(1/\alpha)-O(1)$ for $M$ the packing number of the whole space, and on doubling metrics this is achievable up to an additive $O(dim_D\log\frac{c}{c-1})$. Finally, the space bound is optimal in $k$ and $\alpha$.

item.title: Symbolic forward secrecy analysis of ML-KEM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2787
Authors: Varsha Jarali, Shashi Kant Pandey
Summary: Post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) rely on generic transformations to achieve active security. Specifically, ML-KEM (FIPS 203) applies the Fujisaki--Okamoto (FO) transform to a lattice-based public-key encryption scheme, Kyber.CPAPKE, to construct an IND-CCA2 secure key exchange protocol, ML-KEM. While NIST standards and associated special publications discuss guidelines for establishing larger shared keying material using ML-KEM, formal symbolic proofs to evaluate these operational setups remain sparse. This work addresses this gap by conducting a formal symbolic analysis of ML-KEM using \textsf{ProVerif}. First, we verify the core primitive, establishing symbolic proofs for session key confidentiality, key agreement soundness, and Fujisaki--Okamoto implicit rejection fallback secrecy. Second, we examine the temporal security guarantees of ML-KEM under long-term static key leakage. Using \textsf{ProVerif}'s global phase constructs, we demonstrate that standalone static ML-KEM does not preserve Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), rendering repeated static encapsulation for additional key share establishment vulnerable to retroactive decapsulation. Lastly, we formally model and verify that deploying ML-KEM with ephemeral key rotation or ratcheting mechanisms mitigates this vulnerability, providing robust forward secrecy and complete session domain separation.

item.title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2786
Authors: Eli Goldin, Tomoyuki Morimae
Summary: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required [Malavolta and Walter 2024]. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs): Malavolta and Walter constructed (even everlasting-secure) 2QKE from OWFs [Malavolta and Walter 2024], and Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki, and Yamakawa constructed quantum public-key encryption (QPKE) with quantum public keys, which implies 2QKE, from OWFs [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa 2024]. Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.

item.title: Optimal Early-Stopping Broadcast via Exponential Information Gathering
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2785
Authors: Giovanni Deligios, Fatima Elsheimy, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Ivana Klasovita, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Julian Loss, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: Early-stopping broadcast protocols guarantee termination based on the actual number of malicious parties, $f \leq t$, encountered during execution, rather than the worst-case scenario of $t < n$ corruptions. The seminal work of Dolev, Reischuk, and Strong~[JACM'90] established that $\min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds are necessary. The influential works of Berman, Garay, and Perry~[WDAG'92] and Abraham and Dolev~[STOC'15] introduced the first protocols achieving this optimal bound in the $t < n/3$ (unconditional, no setup) regime, while Perry and Toueg~[Tech.\ Report'84] gave the first protocol for the $t < n/2$ setting (with plain PKI), achieving $2 \cdot \min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds. Despite this early progress, closing the gap to the optimal bound in the computational setting has remained a longstanding open problem, and only recently has progress been made. The best known result in the $t < n/2$ regime is due to Elsheimy, Loss, and Papamanthou~[Eprint'25], achieving $f + O(\sqrt{f})$ rounds. In the dishonest-majority regime, the best known result is due to Deligios, Klasovita, and Liu-Zhang~[Eurocrypt'25], who obtain the first asymptotically optimal protocol, with $O(f)$ round complexity, for $t = (1-\epsilon)n$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a constant.
In this work, we advance the state of the art in two directions. First, in the $t < n/2$ setting with plain PKI, we present a broadcast protocol in which all parties output within optimal $\min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds. Second, we complete the picture by introducing the first protocol that is optimally resilient ($t < n$) and asymptotically matches the lower bound for any number of corruptions $t < n$. By leveraging exponential information gathering (EIG) graphs, our constructions establish that these round bounds are achievable, providing the first feasibility result for optimal-round protocols, albeit at the cost of exponential communication complexity.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Multi-Institutional Clinical Prediction via Multiparty Encrypted Newton-CG Logistic Regression
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2784
Authors: Xiaokang Dai, Weijie Miao, Wenyuan Wu, Yong Feng
Summary: Multi-institutional clinical prediction can benefit from larger and more diverse patient populations, but privacy and data-governance constraints often prevent pooling patient-level records. This study aims to enable collaborative logistic-regression training while keeping such records local. We developed a framework combining multiparty Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) homomorphic encryption with Newton–conjugate gradient optimization. Each institution computes local gradient and damped Hessian contributions, while only encrypted fixed-dimensional statistics are aggregated. The global Newton system is solved by encrypted preconditioned conjugate gradient with diagonal preconditioning and delayed division, making the dominant homomorphic cost depend mainly on model dimension. We evaluated the framework on nine clinical-prediction tasks from NHANES 2017–2018 and on the PIMA Diabetes and Breast Cancer Wisconsin datasets. Across the nine NHANES tasks, mean absolute deviations from pooled-data plaintext Newton training were below 0.002 for area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, area under the precision–recall curve, and average precision. Five-fold cross-validation accuracy was (77.21 ± 1.28)% on PIMA Diabetes and (96.42 ± 1.44)% on Breast Cancer Wisconsin. Under a common 20-iteration budget, the proposed method achieved approximately 3.85× faster training and nearly 90% lower peak memory use than a reproduced multiparty encrypted first-order baseline, while attaining a lower final relative gradient and closer agreement with plaintext Newton. These results show that exploiting locally computed Newton statistics can preserve predictive utility while substantially reducing encrypted training cost, supporting privacy-preserving multi-institutional clinical prediction without pooling patient-level data.

item.title: Bridging Correlation Measures and Unpredictability: Sharp Bounds and Insights for TRNG Validation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2783
Authors: Maciej Skorski, Onur Günlü
Summary: Do small correlations certify high unpredictability? We answer this for the high-order correlation measures (Mauduit and Sárközy) and finite-memory sources.
We develop minimax sharp bounds on next-bit prediction from high-order correlations and show that the min-entropy-rate deficit is linear in the largest correlation, with optimal first-order constants. We also bridge population and sample correlations through ergodic limits and finite-sample guarantees.
As an application, we show that the validation method for true random number generators recently proposed at WAIFI 2026 over-rejects: shrinking (sub-constant) thresholds strongly reject sources of nearly full entropy.

item.title: Memory-Efficient HQC Implementations on Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2782
Authors: Minjoo Sim, Siwoo Eum, Minwoo Lee, Seungwon Lee, Gyeongju Song, Lee Wai Kong, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Hwajeong Seo
Summary: In the Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC) key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), eliminating the polynomial product buffer still leaves serialized inputs, operands, and candidate ciphertexts that may coexist during decapsulation. We organize storage around the last use of each value. Comparing each candidate component before producing the next allows both to share one workspace, while deterministic regeneration shortens the lifetimes of ephemeral supports. Our lifetime analysis relates the measured footprint to the values that coexist during reencryption in our compact design. We read dense operands directly from serialized inputs and reuse output storage as workspace before final serialization during key generation and encapsulation. These choices reduce overlapping storage across the complete KEM and complement established support-form and Zero-Buffer multiplication. We evaluate this organization for all three HQC parameter sets on ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7 under the August 2025 specification. In a cumulative Cortex-M3 HQC-256 comparison, combined representation and lifetime changes reduced the stack by 38.9% relative to a Zero-Buffer configuration that already uses component-wise ciphertext comparison. Using a separate configuration, we measured decapsulation footprints of 36,858 bytes on Cortex-M3 and 36,850 bytes on Cortex-M7, including peak operation stack and serialized input/output storage. The common object layout accounts for most of these footprints. In the evaluated configurations, the relative increase in decapsulation cycles from the direct to the compact implementation is larger on Cortex-M7 than on Cortex-M3. Retaining supports reduces cycles when memory permits. The kernels retain support-dependent control flow and memory accesses; we did not establish complete-KEM constant-time execution or physical side-channel resistance.

item.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2781
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Hyung Tae Lee
Summary: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant.
