As a further application, we also obtain information-theoretic leakage-tolerant circuits against bounded communication leakage, while all prior works are restricted only to the weaker variant of leakage-resilient circuits.

item.title: The Fairest of Them All: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Leader Election
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2738
Authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova, Kelsey Melissaris, Lawrence Roy, Sophia Yakoubov
Summary: Fair leader election is the problem of sampling an unbiased random party out of a set of $n$ parties. The seminal impossibility result of Cleve (STOC 1986) applies to this setting, and shows that the result of the election cannot be unbiased against a dishonest majority. Recent work has achieved the weaker property of game-theoretic fairness, where behaving dishonestly cannot improve one’s chances of being elected. However, such protocols allow even a single corrupt party to bias the outcome. In this work, we introduce best-of-both-worlds (BoBW) fairness, where a small number $t_S$ of corrupt parties cannot bias the result, and even a larger number $t_{GT}$ of corrupt parties still cannot improve their collective election chances (CSP-fairness) nor hurt the election chances of any given honest party (MM-fairness). We present a protocol for BoBW fair leader election for $t_S + t_{GT} < n$. We then prove a generalization of Cleve’s impossibility, and show that this protocol is optimal. Next, in the setting of statistical security we find that BoBW fairness is uninteresting, as it is only possible for an honest majority, where we can get also unbiased leader election. Finally, in the setting of perfect security, we present a BoBW protocol achieving CSP-fairness and strong fairness for $t_S + 1 = t_{CSP} = \frac{n}{3}$, and prove that this is also optimal.

item.title: PS-BKZ: Decoupling Outer Propagation and Local Processing in BKZ by Parameter Separation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2736
Authors: Hutao Song, Hua Guo, Yang Sun, Fengju Gao, Zongyang Zhang, Qianhong Wu
Summary: This work provides a systematic study of parameter separation in Block Korkine–Zolotarev (BKZ) reduction. We propose a general framework with separate parameters for outer propagation and the dominant local computation. The framework covers the local parameter settings of standard BKZ and variants using extended preprocessing, dimensions for free, or progressive sieving, with corresponding adaptations to the outer operations. This allows less expensive local processing without narrowing the outer propagation range.
Within this framework, we give idealized and executable constructions that use inner BKZ with a smaller blocksize to supply local vectors for larger outer blocks. We derive a worst-case quality bound for the idealized construction and analyze its quality–cost behavior using a practical fixed-point model. Experiments on the executable construction cover random q-ary bases up to dimension 300 and SVP Challenge bases up to dimension 240. The detailed comparisons at n ≥ 200 show lower mean root-Hermite factors (RHFs) and 14.1%–59.3% shorter mean running times than BKZ 2.0. Joint improvements generally become more frequent with dimension. On q-ary inputs against BKZ 2.0 with blocksize 50, their frequency increases from 15.56% at n = 150 to 73.33% at n = 300.

item.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2735
Authors: Alessandro Zirilli, Davide Marincione, Evgenios M. Kornaropoulos, Giuseppe Ateniese, Emanuele Rodolà
Summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.

item.title: Finite-Batch q-ary OT Extension for High-Arity Private Lookup: Certified Radix--Code Co-Design
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2734
Authors: Zhuoran Zhang
Summary: High-arity oblivious transfer is a natural abstraction for private lookup: a $\delta$-bit table address selects one entry out of $2^\delta$ candidates. This paper characterizes the finite-batch design space of the CCG q-ary OT-extension family and derives certified radix-selection rules. For $q=2^r$, we formulate radix-code selection as a security-constrained discrete optimization problem that accounts for subfield-check padding, code dimension, required distance, base-OT count, and q-ary symbol width. We derive exact communication thresholds showing when reduced base OTs can compensate for larger q-ary encoding cost. Then we convert the Griesmer bound into communication lower bounds, yielding certificates for regions where non-binary radices cannot improve communication, are provably beneficial, or remain dependent on better code constructions. Finally, we instantiate the framework with simplex and BCH constructions and CodeTables entries, and verify the selected $\delta=12$ codes with Magma.

item.title: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2733
Authors: Nicolas Aragon, Maxime Bros, Ray Perlner, Daniel Smith-Tone, Javier Verbel
Summary: MinRank is an NP-complete problem underlying the security of several post-quantum schemes. It is the hardness assumption of the NIST second-round signature candidate Mirath and of the encryption schemes of Chatterjee et al.\ and Debris-Alazard et al.\ at Eurocrypt 2026. Moreover, it is ubiquitous in the cryptanalysis of multivariate schemes, among them the third-round candidates UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, and SNOVA.
In this work, we revisit the attacks on MinRank. On the combinatorial side, we improve the polynomial part of the kernel-search attack by sharing its linear algebra across guesses, which lowers its cost by 3 to 6 bits on the Mirath parameters and the Courtois challenges, and by up to 3 bits in combination with the hybrid approach. With the improved attack, we solved Courtois challenge~D, open since 2001: an instance over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $19 \times 19$ matrices, $81$ unknowns, and target rank $10$, solved in 11434 CPU days, an estimated $2^{61}$ bit opetations. Our multi-threaded C++ code is publicly available.
On the algebraic side, we show that the complexity of the Kipnis--Shamir (KS) attack is less understood than the literature suggests: the existing estimates rely on a generic Hilbert series that does not predict the rank of the Macaulay matrices of the KS equations. We prove a lower bound on the corank that explains the discrepancy, show that the attack requires a reduced instance with $k \leq m - r$, and derive corrected complexity estimates, which are $1$ to $24$ bits above the best other attack on every Mirath parameter set. We also extend the Support-Minors and Minors modelings with the field equations, which lowers their estimates over small fields: for $q = 2$ and $m = n = 22$, by 9 to 205 bits for Support-Minors and by 17 to 278 bits for Minors. The rank predictions behind the algebraic estimates are stated as assumptions and verified experimentally.

item.title: MuCPay: Breaking the Quadratic Bottleneck in Scriptless Multi-Party Oracle-Based Conditional Payments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2732
Authors: Yaning Wang, Na Wang, Chuan Li, Yongda Zhang, Junsong Fu
Summary: Oracle-based conditional payments triggered by real-world events support decentralized finance applications. However, dense independent bilateral deployments require $\Theta(Nn^2)$ outcome authorizations and $\Theta(n^2)$ settlement signatures for $n$ parties and $N$ outcomes. To go beyond two-party settings, we propose MuCPay, a multi-party oracle-based conditional payment protocol combining (i) $\Theta(Nn)$ off-chain signing shares with one on-chain settlement signature and (ii) BIP340-compatible scriptless settlement on Bitcoin. At its core, MuCPay introduces hash-bound adaptor multi-signatures (HB-AMS) that aggregate parties' conditional authorizations into a compact joint pre-signature. Its single-nonce structure and hash-bound adaptor integration enable efficient multi-party pre-signing. Unlike Double-Layer AMS (EuroS&P'26), HB-AMS produces a standard BIP340 signature under an aggregate public key, enabling direct Taproot key-path settlement. Under static corruption with one honest signer, we prove concurrent new-message unforgeability (CUF) and early-settlement resistance (ES) under our stated algebraic random-oracle model. For 128 parties and 16 outcomes, median complete local preparation takes 2.093 s. For protocol preparation (1.862 s for MuCPay), native-profile projections place VweTS (NDSS’23) and ParaSwap (USENIX’25) work at 1.67 × 10⁴ and 5.05 × 10⁵ times MuCPay's, respectively. Settlement uses one 64-byte signature, while the modeled independent-DLC deployment requires 281.5× as many transaction vbytes. These results demonstrate practical, scalable multi-party oracle-based conditional payments.

item.title: FixSampZ: A Fixed-Point Hardware-Efficient Discrete Gaussian Sampler for Falcon Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2731
Authors: Pushpendra Singh, Akshara K B, Utsav Banerjee, Navin Kashyap
Summary: Falcon, a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature algorithm, offers compact signatures but relies on hardware-intensive floating-point arithmetic. Building on recent theoretical fixed-point formulations, we present a completely floating-point-free hardware architecture for SamplerZ, Falcon’s primary signing bottleneck. By utilizing zero-cost hardware bit-sliced retagging of fixed-point data, which software avoids due to instruction overheads, we enforce tighter data formats at every stage boundary without area or latency penalties. Furthermore, executing floor functions as trivial two's-complement arithmetic right shifts eliminates the complex floor-prediction and redundant data-paths required by floating-point designs. Implemented on UltraScale+ FPGA, our fixed-point sampler exactly matches all 1,024 official test vectors and requires 38% fewer LUTs, 21% less FFs and 36% less DSPs compared to the floating-point baseline, with 21% fewer cycles at a higher clock frequency. We also demonstrate that substituting the baseline ChaCha20 PRNG with lightweight NIST-standardized Ascon-XOF128 achieves further 2-3 × hardware resource savings with zero sampling latency overhead.

item.title: Kaiburr: ML-KEM at (much) higher security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2730
Authors: Swechchha Adhikari, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe
Summary: With deployment of standardized post-quantum cryptography well on the way, discussions continue about concrete choices of schemes and parameter sets. For example, while NIST standardized structured-lattice-based ML-KEM, European agencies like BSI and ANSSI favor unstructured-lattice-based FrodoKEM. Another discussion revolves around different approaches to hybrid deployments – either combining post-quantum schemes with "traditional" elliptic-curve cryptography (or RSA) or combining multiple different post-quantum schemes. The typical question for systems engineers to ask is what the "best" or "most conservative" approach is within a certain performance budget.
In this paper we add a data point to this discussion by investigating how to scale ML-KEM to (much) higher security levels of the underlying MLWE problem. We first observe that increasing security simply by increasing the module rank $k$ quickly reaches a limit imposed by decryption failure probability. We then propose a generalization of the noise distribution, which enables scaling to much larger module rank and MLWE hardness, while preserving the essence of ML-KEM, most notably arithmetic in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256}+1)$ and a simple and constant-time secret / noise generation.
We select three concrete parameter sets of this high-security variant of ML-KEM, which we call Kaiburr. We present benchmarking results for optimized implementations of Kaiburr on 64-bit Intel CPUs and on the Asymmetric Cryptography Coprocessor (ACC) of the Pavona open-source silicon framework. Based on these benchmarks, we argue that, for example, a hybrid of FrodoKEM-976 and Kaiburr-1792 not only offers better performance than FrodoKEM-1344, it also offers protection against a broader range of hypothetical future attacks against (M)LWE.

item.title: Quotienting Redundant Tables: Practical Master-Key Recovery from WBSLT White-Box AES
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2729
Authors: Jiseok Bang, Seungkwang Lee
Summary: Enlarging lookup-table addresses does not hide smaller selectors when the complete public table factors through a core with distinct rows and distinct columns. We demonstrate this condition in WBSLT, a white-box AES design presented at NDSS 2026 that reports resistance to several structural attacks. In the released general generator, the joint output of each group of four first-round TypeII tables has an exact 16 × 16 quotient of its 64 × 64 address space. Mapping its row and column classes to observed addresses recovers the original nibble partition of each AES input byte. Public tables implementing encoded XOR supply compatible output coordinates. Under the generator’s strictly linear input decoder, two 16-point restrictions of each keyed AES S-box then identify its embedded key byte; independent exhaustive checks confirm this property for all 256 byte keys. Using public tables and traces of chosen encoded inputs, we recover every key in 200 general instances that passed 200,000 reference AES block tests, after a median of 146 and at most 221 inputs. Separate 200-instance cohorts of the released optimized C source and its one-line functional repair also yield every key; only the repair passes the AES tests. An adjacent-round adaptation recovers 20/20 exact keys on a paired cohort without reconstructing the nibble partition. On those instances, our first-round route uses fewer live trace queries and less public table data. The exact quotient provides a concrete test for selector partitions that survive address enlargement.

item.title: Tight Depth Lower Bounds for Stretch Amplification
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2728
Authors: Oliver Korten
Summary: We investigate the depth overhead of stretch-amplification for pseudorandom generators in the black-box model. We show that any black box construction of a PRG $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which makes $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ queries to a PRG $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ in $d$ adaptive phases during each evaluation (and with a black-box reduction to the security of $G$) must satisfy: $M \leq (m + O(\log n)) \Bigl( \frac{N}{n - O(\log n)} \Bigr)^d$. This implies that the standard amplification procedure [GM'84, GGM'86] based on repeated composition of $G$ is essentially optimal. In particular, amplifying $n \mapsto n+1$ to $m \mapsto 2m$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\frac{n}{\log n})$, and amplifying $n \mapsto 2n$ to $m \mapsto m^2$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\log n)$; each of these bounds is tight up to a constant factor. As an immediate corollary we obtain tight lower bounds on the depth complexity of black-box constructions of PRFs from PRGs. Both of these problems (pertaining to amplification and PRF construction) have been studied in various prior works [V'05, MV'11, BJP'11, MV'15, BMM'24, ADV'26]. Despite progress on special cases in which the structure of the reductions is constrained, it was previously unknown whether completely parallel constructions ($d=1$) existed in every stretch regime.
The kinds of amplification procedures we investigate have more recently found use outside of cryptography in the study of range avoidance ("Avoid") [K'21]. We show an analogous result in this setting: any black-box $\mathrm{FP^{NP}}$ reduction from an Avoid instance $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ to a second Avoid instance $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which has "depth $d$" in the above sense must satisfy the same bound relating $n,N,m,M,d$. Using this impossibility result for Avoid, we construct an oracle relative to which $\mathrm{E} \not\subseteq \mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$ but $\mathrm{E^{NP}} \subseteq \mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$. Our oracle separation implies that in the relativized setting, the bounded arithmetic theory $S^1_2$ cannot prove the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$, even given as an axiom the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$.
